title: 第十九章 半个先生
content_zh:
练字驯心是慢功夫，可肚子不等人。

    秦伯一个游方郎中，自己都是吃了上顿没下顿。江砚再添一张嘴，破庙里那点粮米，眼看着就见了底。江砚心里过意不去，琢磨着得自己找条活路。

    可他能干什么？

    一身的力气，是没有的——这具身子瘦得风一吹就倒，挑担、扛货、拉车，干不动。手艺，更谈不上。他一个穿越来的大学生，前世除了会敲键盘、考试，半点能在这世道换饭吃的本事都没有。

    思来想去，他就剩一样东西：识字。

    这念头是在坊市里冒出来的。

    那天他替秦伯去抓药，路过城东的市集。市集口蹲着个写字摊，一个穿长衫的落魄秀才，面前摆张矮桌，桌上笔墨纸砚，旁边竖块布招子，写着“代写书信，记账算数“。一个赶车的汉子蹲在他对面，红着脸，结结巴巴地说，那秀才提笔就写。

    江砚站在边上看了半晌。

    那汉子是要给在外当兵的儿子捎封信。说不出什么文绉绉的话，就是翻来覆去那几句：“家里都好，别惦记““你娘的咳嗽好些了““今年收成薄，省着点花“。秀才听一句，写一句，写完念给汉子听，汉子听一句，点一下头，眼圈就红一分。

    写完，汉子从怀里掏出三个铜钱，恭恭敬敬放下，作了个揖，才走。

    三个铜钱。

    江砚的心，动了一下。

    他识字。他不光识这大胤的字——原主在私塾旁听过，认得些；他自己穿越来，连蒙带猜，加上这些天就着字帖练，认的字只多不少。算数他更不怵，前世那点加减乘除，碾压这市井里的算盘账，绰绰有余。

    写信，记账，算数。

    这不正是他能干的么？

    回去他跟秦伯一说。

    秦伯正眯着眼晒太阳，听完，睁开眼，上下打量他一回，忽然笑了。

    “你也想去摆摊代写？”老人捋了捋胡子，“行啊。识字的人，在这世道，到底比睁眼瞎强。”他顿了顿，又笑，“就你这半桶水，能写明白家信、记清楚流水账，也算个……半个先生了。”

    半个先生。

    江砚被这称呼逗笑了。可心里，竟有点说不出的踏实。

    从废柴，到逃奴，到现在，总算有个能拿来糊口、还不算丢人的名头了。

    他没钱置办那秀才那样的体面行头。一方砚、一锭墨、一支秃笔，是秦伯翻箱底翻出来给他的；纸，是他厚着脸皮去纸铺，赊了最便宜的草纸；桌子，是捡的一块破门板，下头垫两块砖。布招子也没有，他就在门板上，用炭歪歪扭扭——不，是工工整整地，写了八个字：

    代写书信记账算数。
content_en:
Practicing calligraphy and taming the mind is a slow process, but the stomach waits for no one.

    Uncle Qin is a wandering doctor, and he has always had one meal but no one. Jiang Yan opened his mouth again, and saw that the little grain and rice in the ruined temple were all gone. Jiang Yan felt guilty and thought about finding a way to survive on his own.

    But what can he do?

    There is no strength in the whole body - this body is so thin that it will collapse when the wind blows. It cannot carry burdens, carry goods, or pull carts. Not to mention craftsmanship. He is a college student who came from time-travel. In his previous life, apart from being able to type on the keyboard and take exams, he had no ability at all to make a living in this world.

    After much thought, he only had one thing left: literacy.

    This idea came to me in Fangshi.

    That day he went to grab medicine for Uncle Qin and passed by the market in the east of the city. There was a writing stall squatting at the entrance of the market. A down-and-out scholar in a long gown had a low table in front of him. On the table was a pen, ink, paper and inkstone. Next to it was a piece of cloth with the words "Write letters, keep accounts and do calculations". A man driving a carriage squatted opposite him, blushing and stammering, "The scholar started writing as soon as he picked up his pen."

    Jiang Yan stood aside and watched for a long time.

    The man wanted to send a letter to his son who was serving as a soldier outside. I couldn't say anything literate, I just kept repeating the following sentences: "Everything is fine at home, don't worry about it." "Your mother's cough is better." "This year's harvest is small, so save some flowers." The scholar listens to a sentence, writes a sentence, and after writing, reads it to the man. The man listens to a sentence, nods his head, and his eye circles become red.

    After finishing writing, the man took out three copper coins from his arms, put them down respectfully, bowed before leaving.

    Three copper coins.

    Jiang Yan's heart moved.

    He can read. Not only did he recognize Dayin's calligraphy - the original owner heard it in a private school and recognized it a little bit; he traveled back in time himself and even guessed it, and he had been practicing with copybooks these days, so he could only recognize a lot more characters. He is not afraid of arithmetic. The addition, subtraction, multiplication and division he had in his previous life was more than enough to crush the abacus accounts in this market.

    Write letters, keep accounts, do math.

    Isn't this what he can do?

    He told Uncle Qin when he got back.

    Uncle Qin was basking in the sun with his eyes squinted. After listening, he opened his eyes, looked him up and down, and suddenly smiled.

    "You also want to set up a stall to write for yourself?" The old man stroked his beard, "Okay. In this world, a literate person is better than being blind." He paused and then smiled, "You are half a bucket of water. If you can write family letters clearly and remember journals clearly, you can be considered... half a gentleman."

    Half a gentleman.

    Jiang Yan was amused by this title. But in my heart, I felt a little unspeakably at ease.

    From good-for-nothing, to a runaway slave, now, he finally has a name that he can use to make a living, which is not embarrassing.

    He didn't have the money to buy decent attire like that scholar. An inkstone, an ingot of ink, and a bare pen were given to him by Uncle Qin who rummaged through the box; the paper was given to him by him shamelessly going to the paper shop and getting the cheapest straw paper on credit; the table was a broken door panel with two bricks underneath. He didn't have any tricks, so he just used charcoal to crumble - no, neatly - and wrote eight words on the door panel:

    Write letters and keep accounts.
